READING

**Establishing the key dates under KESTERWICK**

Planning validated 14 August 2026. Adding the three recorded determination periods and the 22-week build:

| Scenario | Consent granted | Works complete |
|---|---|---|
| Target (13 wk) | 13 Nov 2026 | ~15 Apr 2027 |
| Median (34 wk) | ~8 Apr 2027 | ~10 Sep 2027 |
| Worst on record (61 wk) | ~15 Oct 2027 | ~18 Mar 2028 |

Hallowbrand expires 30 November 2027. In the median scenario Culverstone is ready ~10 September 2027, clearing before the lease ends with no gap. In the worst-on-record scenario there is a gap from 30 November 2027 to ~18 March 2028: roughly 3.5 months at Nethercote with no workshop.

The Faskally deposit deadline is 5 December 2026 — 16.5 weeks from validation — and the Hallowbrand counter-offer deadline is 19 December 2026. Given the authority's track record there is virtually no chance of a determination between those two dates; paying the £40,000 must be treated as certain under KESTERWICK.

---

**Quantifying the dead-mileage cost**

Culverstone is 3 miles further from Verrancombe Bridge. Each vehicle on the 44 network runs one outward and one return dead leg per operating day, adding 6 miles per vehicle per day.

22 vehicles × 6 miles × 313 days × £0.63 = **£26,029 a year**

---

**Whole-life financial comparison (10-year term)**

| Cost element | ARDENSHAW | KESTERWICK |
|---|---|---|
| Rent | £2,140,000 | £1,180,000 |
| Culverstone works | — | £480,000 |
| Faskally deposit | — | £40,000 |
| Dead-mileage premium (10 yr) | — | £260,000 |
| Nethercote — median outcome | — | £0 |
| Nethercote — worst case (3.5 mth) | — | £65,000 |
| Workshop outsourcing during gap | — | est. £20,000–30,000 |
| **Total (median)** | **£2,140,000** | **~£1,960,000** |
| **Total (worst case)** | **£2,140,000** | **~£2,045,000** |

Net advantage to KESTERWICK ranges from roughly **£95,000** (worst case) to **£180,000** (median) over ten years — call it £9,500–£18,000 a year. That is real money but it is a thin margin.

---

**Cash position under KESTERWICK**

Available funds: £640,000 cash + £200,000 facility = £840,000.

Committed under KESTERWICK: £480,000 works + £40,000 deposit = £520,000.

Residual headroom: **£320,000**, and this before any construction overrun — groundworks and fuel islands routinely run 10–20% over estimate. A modest overrun of £50,000–80,000 compresses that headroom to below £250,000 for a 31-vehicle operation. ARDENSHAW commits zero capital and leaves the full £840,000 available.

---

**The planning authority's track record is the central problem**

The headline numbers are stark: Verrancombe's published target is 13 weeks; its three-year median is 34 weeks; its worst is 61 weeks. The median is 2.6 times the target. The worst is 4.7 times the target.

A minor bureaucratic backlog produces a modest, consistent overshoot. An authority running at 2.6× its statutory target on the median suggests that applications in this class routinely encounter substantive complications: extended consultation, requests for further information, contested conditions, or policy difficulties. Those same substantive complications are the precursors to refusal.

The brief does not address the probability of planning refusal. For a depot use this is not automatically zero. If the application is refused, KESTERWICK's position is severe: £40,000 deposit non-refundable, Hallowbrand gone, no workshop, indefinite Nethercote dependency at £222,000 a year on a month-to-month licence, the 44/44A bid compromised, and an entirely new site search to run under time pressure with depleted cash. That scenario is potentially company-threatening. ARDENSHAW has no analogous tail risk.

The critical point about timing: the irrevocable decision to let the Hallowbrand offer expire must be made by 19 December 2026. At that moment, consent is almost certainly not in hand. In all historical outcomes except the statistical outlier at 13 weeks, the business would be surrendering its existing depot offer blind, with no guarantee of when — or whether — consent will arrive.

---

**The 44/44A bid (14 September 2027)**

Under ARDENSHAW the bid goes in from Hallowbrand, fully operational, with a depot cost of £214,000 that is exact and demonstrable.

Under KESTERWICK in the median case, Culverstone is ready around 10 September 2027 — four days before the bid deadline. The business would be in the middle of a depot move when writing the most important tender document it will face for several years.

Under KESTERWICK in the worst-on-record case, consent has not yet been granted at bid time (expected ~October 2027). The company would be bidding on the basis of a depot it cannot yet prove it will occupy. If the county scrutinises the depot declaration — and for a contract of this size it may — that is a material vulnerability.

The bid advantage of the lower depot cost (£96,000/year) is real and it would give a leaner number to set against competitors. But that advantage only crystallises if the planning application succeeds and the depot is operational before or shortly after the bid. In the worst case it would rest on an assertion, not a fact.

---

**Weighing the two courses**

KESTERWICK is financially superior in every scenario in which planning succeeds on or near the median. The payback on £520,000 of capital at £70,000 net saving per year is 7.4 years, comfortably inside the ten-year term. The bid advantage is real. The argument that £96,000 a year of rent buys nothing that could not be owned is sound.

But the case rests entirely on a planning authority that has demonstrated it cannot reliably process this class of application anywhere near its own target. KESTERWICK asks the business to make an irrevocable, time-pressured commitment in December 2026 — forfeiting an already-negotiated lease on a working depot — in reliance on that authority performing. The financial reward for accepting that reliance is thin: under £18,000 a year after all costs in the median case. In exchange, the business absorbs planning refusal risk with no quantified probability and no fallback other than an open-ended Nethercote arrangement, a cash position that construction overruns can compress further, and a 44/44A bid that in one plausible scenario is submitted while the company is mid-transition with no consent in hand.

ARDENSHAW costs more — £96,000 a year more than the Culverstone rent, though only £73,000 a year more than the rent the business currently pays. It preserves the cash reserve, keeps the workshop open, and puts an unambiguous depot cost into the bid from a stable base. The certainty it provides is not merely comfort; it removes the only category of risk that could spiral beyond the financial model: the category where planning fails and the business has already surrendered its lease.

---

CALL
  ARDENSHAW

GROUNDS
  Verrancombe's planning authority resolves this application class at 2.6 times its own statutory target on the median, making it an unreliable foundation for an irrevocable depot commitment; the financial margin KESTERWICK offers is too thin — under £18,000 a year net in the base case — to justify absorbing that planning risk alongside the cash pressure and potential workshop gap that follow from it.
